Traditional Knowledge

Timekeeping Before Clocks: How India and Bengal Told the Time

Proteeti Satpati Jun 4 4 min read

“Time was once told by tides and twilight, sung by birds, and whispered by the wind, long before clocks dared to measure it.”

Long before the mechanical clock, people found their own ways to track time. They watched the sky. They built water clocks. The need to plan daily life, farming and rituals gave rise to unique ways of keeping time.

This was true for India, and especially Bengal. People here built their days around local ways of telling time. These mixed science with ritual, and nature with culture. In this post, we look at how people in Bengal and the wider Indian subcontinent knew the hour. We cover star calculations, water clocks, temple bells and birdcalls. We also look at how these old methods still live on in cultural practice, even against the relentless pace of machines today.

Reading the Sky: Astronomy and the Panchang

Astronomy was central to timekeeping in India and Bengal. People watched the sun, moon and stars closely. They charted their movements to split days and years into useful units. Bengal, with its strong tradition of astronomy and maths, added a lot to this early work. The Panchang was the traditional Hindu calendar. It used the lunar cycle to divide the year into months named after major constellations. It shows how much the Nakshatras and other heavenly bodies shaped rituals, farming and government.

For centuries, Bengali scholars and priests used the Panchang to pick auspicious days for festivals and farming cycles. Bengali astronomers like Raghunath Purushottama refined these calculations to make more accurate almanacs for daily life. This gave us ideas like Tithis (lunar days) and Muhurats (auspicious time periods). Both were widely used for religious and social events.

Bangabda: Akbar’s Blended Calendar

Another landmark in Bengal’s pre-clock history was the Bengali calendar, the Bangabda. Akbar introduced it in 1584. It blended Islamic lunar and Hindu solar ways of keeping time. This helped standardise timekeeping in Bengal, especially for farming. It lined up tax collection with the region’s seasons.

Ghati Yantra: Telling Time with Water

People also built the Ghati system. These were water clocks called Ghati Yantras. They measured time by letting water flow at a set rate from one vessel to another, in units called Ghatikas. The Dakshineshwar and Kalighat temples used them to signal daily prayer and offering times. They also helped regulate trade and administrative work in the medieval cities of Murshidabad and Gauda.

Nature as a Clock: Cues from the Land and Water

In this period, people in Bengal also leaned on nature to tell time. The call of the cuckoo signalled dawn. The tides told the fishermen of the Sundarbans when to set out. The boatmen’s Bhatiyali songs often spoke of time and how it waits for no one. Even the sacred Brahma Muhurta (the religiously important pre-dawn hour) was set by the movement of the stars and the symbolic quiet of the natural world. In short, Bengal’s life on the water shaped everything. Rivers such as the Ganges, the Hooghly and the Brahmaputra guided trade, travel and daily life.

Bells and Criers: Sound as a Signal

No account of timekeeping in Bengal is complete without bells, an age-old way of signalling time. Temples big and small rang bells for Mangal Arati and midday offerings. In trade towns like Kolkata and Chandannagar, bells marked when markets opened and closed. Public criers often rang bells to announce big events and mark the time for shared activities.

The Colonial Shift: From Cycles to Clocks

The British brought European clocks. Almost ominously, these called time on every way of keeping time the land had known. Water clocks gave way to Big Ben-style clock towers. Wristwatches replaced sundials. Bit by bit, local methods gave way to machines, and modern inventions overtook traditional knowledge.

Echoes in the Present: Traditional Time Lives On

But not all is lost. Traditional lunar calendars are still a must in Bengali homes. They matter most when picking auspicious days for sacred rituals and festivals. This shows that ancient timekeeping has itself stood the test of time. In a world that runs more and more on machines, these methods still hold their place. They remind us of the deep bond between people and nature, the cleverness of ancient science, and the cultural rhythms that still shape our lives.

Timekeeping is not just science. It is woven deep into Bengali social life. It has quietly endured in a race set by the beat of quartz and atomic seconds. It survives in the ringing of temple bells, the rhythm of the tides, and the rustle of Bengali calendars in every Bengali drawing room. By preserving these practices and knowledge, we honour rhythm over rush, and community over clockwork.
